architectural_implications.after: A context engine resolves task-specific flows and hands precise, sequenced context to the agent via MCP/Claude Code or Slack.
architectural_implications.before: Engineer manually gathers context in the IDE; agent receives whatever is pasted or searched via MCP.
architectural_implications.consequence: A new service boundary with its own indexing, correlation (PR↔Slack), and ranking (seniority) responsibilities — and a new failure domain between agent and repo.
architectural_implications.observation: Context provision is being extracted from the human-in-the-loop and from the model prompt into a dedicated engine sitting between agents and organizational knowledge stores.

architectural_implications.after: Curate and route only the information a specific task requires, with explicit sequencing.
architectural_implications.before: Dump the codebase and docs into the context window, or let the agent search freely.
architectural_implications.consequence: Retrieval must be task-aware; evaluation must be task-scoped, and index design must support dependency tracing rather than similarity search alone.
architectural_implications.observation: The unit of retrieval shifts from documents/chunks to task-specific flows.

architectural_implications.after: The context engine returns a step-by-step sequencing plan with precise file references.
architectural_implications.before: The agent scans files to discover call paths and ordering.
architectural_implications.consequence: Reduces exploratory tool calls and token burn, and makes plans auditable against a context source independent of the agent.
architectural_implications.observation: Dependency tracing and sequencing plans become a first-class output of the context layer, not of the coding agent.

architectural_implications.after: Seniority and expertise signals boost specific comments in review context.
architectural_implications.before: All retrieved comments and docs treated as equal-signal text.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires an engineering social graph and identity data as a dependency of the context engine, plus governance over how authority is inferred.
architectural_implications.observation: Authority/expertise weighting is injected into the retrieval ranking function.

article_ideas.angle: Architectural argument: contrast the tool-access boundary (MCP) with a selection/sequencing boundary, and show why bigger context windows and broader retrieval cannot fix premature termination.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and platform architects building agent stacks on MCP
article_ideas.based_on: Access to information does not equal understanding
article_ideas.thesis: Building an agent stack on raw MCP access bakes the 'satisfaction of search' failure mode into the architecture: unbounded search over a corpus systematically under-retrieves and terminates at the first plausible hit, so the missing layer is task-scoped routing and sequencing, not a larger index.
article_ideas.title: MCP Gives Your Agent Access. It Does Not Give It Understanding.

article_ideas.angle: Metrics critique: reframe agent evaluation around a production gate and argue that plausible-but-unmergeable output is the failure mode benchmark suites are blind to.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, DevEx/platform teams, and agent-evaluation practitioners
article_ideas.thesis: Compile success and plausibility are proxy metrics that hide the dominant downstream cost of agent-written code; review acceptance and rework rate at the merge gate are the metrics that actually track whether a context layer paid for itself.
article_ideas.title: Measure at the Merge Gate, Not the Compiler

article_ideas.angle: Diagnostic reframe plus honest caveat — the level distribution is asserted without instrumentation data, so propose measurable criteria per level instead of accepting the taxonomy.
article_ideas.audience: CTOs, platform leads, and engineering managers planning AI adoption
article_ideas.based_on: Most engineering organizations are currently stuck at levels 4 to 5
article_ideas.thesis: Engineering organizations stall not because models are too weak but because context provisioning never graduates from human-in-the-loop to an engineered layer; reading the maturity curve as a roadmap of relocating context work out of prompts and people gives a more actionable diagnostic than capability ladders.
article_ideas.title: The Maturity Axis Nobody Names: Who Supplies the Context

connections.relationship: A diagnostic/perception bias pattern transposed onto agent search: both describe premature commitment to a first satisfying signal, suggesting termination criteria should be explicit rather than model-judged.
Complementary but competing layers: MCP supplies access, the context engine supplies selection and sequencing; the claim is that access alone is not sufficient.

connections.connects_to: who supplies context (human vs curated vs engineered layer)
connections.relationship: The taxonomy's implicit axis is the locus of context responsibility, making it a roadmap for relocating context work out of humans and prompts into infrastructure.
Proposes review-pass/merge rate as the target metric instead of compile success or plausibility, tying agent evaluation to a production gate.
Identity and expertise data becomes an input to retrieval scoring, linking org-chart-like data to context precision.

evidence_quotes.text: Access to information does not equal understanding.
Radiologist finding one cancer indicator and missing others; agents finding one piece of info and stopping prematurely.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent system whose knowledge interface is 'search the corpus' will systematically under-retrieve and stop at the first satisfying hit; the fix is a curated routing layer that enumerates what a task requires, not a bigger index or larger context window.
core_insights.insight: Raw MCP access to repos and docs is architecturally insufficient: it provides retrieval ability without holistic understanding, and agents exhibit a 'satisfaction of search' failure mode — finding one plausible piece of evidence and terminating the search prematurely.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes the tool-access layer as the wrong abstraction boundary: unbounded search over a corpus is not the same as an understanding layer that routes task-specific context. Teams building agent stacks on MCP servers alone are building the failure mode into the architecture.

evidence_quotes.text: Without upfront context preparation, agents iterate on wrong assumptions, leading to compounding token costs and repeated human intervention.
Cost comparison showing session usage with Unblocked (~$0.93, 1 min) versus without Unblocked (~$1.22, 2 mins).

core_insights.generalization: For multi-step agent tasks, per-iteration cost is dominated by the correctness of initial assumptions; investing in retrieval precision at step zero reduces total tokens and wall-clock superlinearly with iteration count.
core_insights.insight: Context failures compound in cost rather than staying constant: agents iterate on wrong assumptions, driving repeated human intervention and multiplied token spend, so pre-task context curation is cheaper than post-hoc correction.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete economic argument for investing in a context layer upstream of the agent loop instead of paying for retries and human triage downstream — a cost model that changes where budget is spent in agent harness design.

evidence_quotes.text: Levels 1-2: Tab complete, Agent IDE (You are the context layer).
Levels 3-4: Context engineering, Parallel agents (Curated context).
Most engineering organizations are currently stuck at levels 4 to 5 and treat context as the primary bottleneck.

core_insights.generalization: Agent-system maturity can be characterized by whether context is supplied by a human in the loop, curated ahead of time, or provisioned by an engineered layer — an axis usable for roadmapping any agent platform.
core_insights.insight: An AI maturity taxonomy where the differentiator between stages is *who supplies context*: at levels 1-2 the human is the context layer, at 3-4 context is curated, at 5-6 a context layer plus harness engineering exists. The bottleneck is treated as context rather than model capability.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Provides an adoption diagnostic that locates teams on a capability axis defined by context supply, and claims most organizations stall at levels 4-5 — implying the binding constraint in industry practice is context infrastructure, not model quality.

evidence_quotes.text: Seniority and expertise signals are used to boost important comments in code reviews.
Debugging why code review issues dropped using Slack conversation threads correlated with PRs.

core_insights.generalization: Where decision rationale lives outside artifacts (chat, review comments, incident threads), any context engine needs both a correlation mechanism linking those channels to artifacts and an authority ranking, otherwise it retrieves opinion without weighting it.
core_insights.insight: Organizational intelligence for code review extends beyond source code into communication history: correlating GitHub PRs with Slack threads, and weighting comments by seniority/expertise signals from an engineering social graph, improves review relevance.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Suggests the retrieval corpus for engineering agents should include conversational and social-signal data, not just code and docs — a non-obvious expansion of what counts as context, and one that requires an identity/authority model layered over the retrieval index.

evidence_quotes.text: AI-generated code should feel like it was written by someone who has been on your team for years, but it doesn't today.
Without context, agents produce plausible output that compiles but fails human review and real-world expectations.

core_insights.generalization: Agent quality for production code should be measured at the merge gate — review acceptance, rework rate — because plausible-but-unmergeable output carries hidden downstream cost that compile-based benchmarks miss.
core_insights.insight: The stated goal state is not merely better completion but 'mergeable' code — output that survives human review — which makes review-pass rate the operative quality metric rather than compile success or plausibility.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Distinguishes a metric that matters operationally (does the diff get merged) from proxy metrics (does it compile, does it look plausible), and frames the failure mode as output that 'compiles but fails human review'.

evidence_quotes.text: AI agents treated as new employees reset their knowledge every time they start a new task, lacking tribal knowledge, past decisions, architecture rationale, and incident history.
For years, humans have been the context layer.

core_insights.generalization: Treat the context layer as durable organizational state separate from the agent session, so that knowledge survives model swaps, context resets, and task boundaries.
core_insights.insight: Agents are stateless across tasks in the way a new hire is contextless: every task re-triggers onboarding into codebase, test suites, deployment patterns, and past architectural decisions.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Reframes persistent context as an onboarding artifact owned by the organization rather than a conversation-level memory feature owned by the agent — different owner, different lifecycle, different interface.

deep_dives.why: If the failure mode is premature commitment to the first satisfying hit, the fix is a harness-level constraint rather than a bigger index or a larger context window — which changes what a context layer must emit (coverage assertions, required-evidence sets) instead of merely returning ranked chunks.

evidence_quotes.text: Access to information does not equal understanding.
Dumping an entire codebase and all docs into a context window causes agent distraction and wastes tokens.
Task-specific flow is required to prevent agents from getting distracted.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Access to information does not equal understanding
deep_dives.why: The distinction between 'access' and 'understanding' is the central claim of the talk but is never mechanized; an ablation separates routing/decomposition effects from retrieval-quality effects and tells builders which layer to invest in first.

deep_dives.why: If cost is superlinear in assumption error, then cheap-but-wrong first context is not merely suboptimal but structurally more expensive than curated context, which is a concrete budget-allocation rule for agent harness design rather than a slogan.

Debugging why code review issues dropped using Slack conversation threads correlated with PRs.

project_ideas.poc: Run three arms on one fixed task suite over a frozen corpus: raw MCP free search; tuned hybrid retrieval with no task routing; task-decomposed routing that emits a step-by-step sequencing plan with file references. Hold model and cache state constant.

project_ideas.based_on: Cost comparison showing session usage with Unblocked
project_ideas.hypothesis: The reported ~50% token reduction from a context layer persists across a fixed multi-task suite under controlled cache state and task equivalence, with effect size smaller than the single-demo figure but still directionally significant.
project_ideas.measurement: Mean and variance of tokens and wall-clock per task, cost per completed task, and the fraction of the reported reduction surviving controls for caching and task equivalence.
project_ideas.name: Context-Layer Cost Trial Protocol
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a Claude Code workflow with an A/B harness that pins task equivalence, cache state, and complexity labels, then replays each task with and without the context layer for N repetitions, logging token usage, wall-clock, and a cost-equivalent figure.

project_ideas.based_on: Seniority and expertise signals are used to boost important comments in code reviews.

project_ideas.measurement: Comment retrieval precision/recall against ground-truth outcomes, merge acceptance of agent changes, and precision degradation as a function of authority-weight strength.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Peter Werry
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Context engines for AI software engineering agents and the limitations of raw MCP access versus organizational context layers.
  • Purpose: To demonstrate how a context engine bridges the gap between AI agents and organizational knowledge, reducing token waste, hallucinations, and code review friction. Peter Werry, co-founder of Unblocked, explains why AI coding agents fail to produce production-grade mergeable code without an organizational context layer. He explores the AI maturity curve in engineering organizations, contrasts access to tools with actual understanding, demonstrates a live demo of the Unblocked context engine integrated with Claude Code and Slack/GitHub, and analyzes token usage and efficiency tradeoffs.

Topic Map

The Problem: Agents Lack Organizational Context

  • Explanation: AI agents treated as new employees reset their knowledge every time they start a new task, lacking tribal knowledge, past decisions, architecture rationale, and incident history.
  • Key claims:
    • AI-generated code should feel like it was written by someone who has been on your team for years, but it doesn't today.
    • For years, humans have been the context layer.
    • Now your agents have the same problem. Only the cost compounds.
  • Examples:
    • Searching across outdated docs, Notion, Slack discussions, Confluence, and GitHub pull requests to figure out how auth validation works.
  • Terminology:
    • context engine
    • organizational context
    • tribal knowledge
    • AI maturity curve
  • Why it matters: Without context, agents produce plausible output that compiles but fails human review and real-world expectations.

Levels of AI Maturity in Engineering Organizations

  • Explanation: A taxonomy of engineering organization maturity ranging from basic tab completion to fully autonomous software factories.
  • Key claims:
    • Levels 1-2: Tab complete, Agent IDE (You are the context layer).
    • Levels 3-4: Context engineering, Parallel agents (Curated context).
    • Levels 5-6: MCP + skills, Harness engineering (Context layer).
    • Levels 7-8: Cloud agents, Software factories.
  • Examples:
    • Moving from GitHub Copilot tab-complete up to automated software factories.
  • Terminology:
    • AI maturity curve
    • MCP
    • context layer
    • software factories
  • Why it matters: Most engineering organizations are currently stuck at levels 4 to 5 and treat context as the primary bottleneck.

Access Does Not Equal Understanding

  • Explanation: Connecting agents to Model Context Protocols (MCP) gives them access to code and docs, but suffers from 'satisfaction of search' similar to radiologists stopping at one X-ray indicator.
  • Key claims:
    • Access to information does not equal understanding.
    • Dumping an entire codebase and all docs into a context window causes agent distraction and wastes tokens.
    • Task-specific flow is required to prevent agents from getting distracted.
  • Examples:
    • Radiologist finding one cancer indicator and missing others; agents finding one piece of info and stopping prematurely.
  • Terminology:
    • satisfaction of search
    • context window
    • task-specific flow
  • Why it matters: Unstructured massive context dumps lead to wasted tokens, distracted agents, and operating on wrong assumptions.

Live Demo: Unblocked with Claude Code and Slack

  • Explanation: Demonstrating how querying Unblocked directly in Slack or inside Claude Code yields architecturally sound plans, dependency tracing, and accurate context retrieval.
  • Key claims:
    • Unblocked generates internal diagrams and architectural proposals by understanding code changes and past discussions.
    • Using Unblocked with Claude Code results in ~50% fewer tokens, faster triage, and better answers.
    • Seniority and expertise signals are used to boost important comments in code reviews.
  • Examples:
    • Asking how the SourceMark engine works and getting a generated pipeline diagram and step-by-step sequencing plan.
    • Debugging why code review issues dropped using Slack conversation threads correlated with PRs.
  • Terminology:
    • SourceMark engine
    • Context Engine Simulator
    • code review agent
    • engineering social graph
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates measurable cost and time reductions when pairing coding agents with an active context layer.

Key Points

Agents as New Employees

  • Explanation: AI coding agents reset their knowledge on every new task, requiring rediscovery of codebases, test suites, and deployment patterns.
  • Evidence: Analogy comparing agents to expert software engineers who onboard for the first time on every task.
  • Practical implication: Engineering teams must provide persistent context layers to prevent repetitive onboarding overhead.

Access vs Understanding

  • Explanation: Giving agents raw access to repos via MCPs allows them to search, but they lack holistic understanding of architectural dependencies.
  • Evidence: Radiology analogy of 'satisfaction of search' where finding one indicator causes an agent to stop searching.
  • Practical implication: Context engines must curate and route precise information rather than dumping raw codebases into context windows.

Compounding Cost of Contextless Agents

  • Explanation: Without upfront context preparation, agents iterate on wrong assumptions, leading to compounding token costs and repeated human intervention.
  • Evidence: Cost comparison showing session usage with Unblocked (~$0.93, 1 min) versus without Unblocked (~$1.22, 2 mins).
  • Practical implication: Context layers save significant token costs and wall-clock time on complex multi-step coding tasks.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Levels of AI Maturity in Engineering Organizations

  • How it works: Categorizes adoption from simple auto-complete to autonomous software factories based on how context is provided to developers and agents.
  • Components:
    • Tab complete
    • Agent IDE
    • Context engineering
    • Parallel agents
    • MCP + skills
    • Harness engineering
    • Cloud agents
    • Software factories
  • When to use: To evaluate an engineering team's current readiness and identify bottlenecks in AI adoption.

Examples & Case Studies

Asking Claude Code to optimize the SourceMark calculator scheduler with and without Unblocked context.

  • Illustrates: The difference in plan quality, precision of file references, and token efficiency when using an organizational context engine.
  • Lesson: Context engines provide precise sequencing plans that avoid unnecessary file scanning and reduce token consumption.

Analyzing a drop in weekly code review issues by correlating GitHub pull requests with Slack conversations.

  • Illustrates: How unblocked code review agents leverage historical team conversations and seniority signals.
  • Lesson: Organizational intelligence extends beyond source code into team communication history.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Evaluate your team's position on the AI maturity curve.
    • Recognize that raw MCP access to code and docs is insufficient for autonomous agents.
    • Test the Context Engine Simulator to measure token and quality differences.
  • Strategic:
    • Build or adopt a dedicated context layer to prevent agents from resetting knowledge per task.
    • Incorporate organizational metadata (Slack, PRs, Notion docs) into agent execution workflows.
    • Leverage engineering social graphs to weight code review expertise and intent.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can we minimize token costs while scaling agent context windows?
    • What data sources provide the highest signal-to-noise ratio for our engineering agents?
    • How do we maintain security and privacy when feeding organizational chat history into context layers?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Using Unblocked with Claude Code results in ~50% fewer tokens and faster triage. (Performance metric)
  • Context engines reduce session costs from $1.22 to $0.93 on complex refactoring tasks. (Cost comparison)

Notable Quotes

"AI-generated code should feel like it was written by someone who's been on your team for years. But it doesn't today." "For years, you have been the context layer." "Now your agents have the same problem. Only the cost compounds." "Access to information does not equal understanding." "-50% fewer tokens, faster triage, and Unblocked's answer was actually better because it wasn't buried in noise."

Compressed Summary

  • AI agents suffer from onboarding amnesia on every new task.
  • Raw MCP access to code and docs leads to distraction and 'satisfaction of search'.
  • Unblocked's context engine integrates Slack, GitHub, Notion, and Confluence into agent workflows.
  • Context engines reduce token usage by ~50% and wall-clock execution time.
  • Engineering social graphs capture tribal knowledge and team seniority signals.
  • Keywords: context engine, ai agents, mcp, code review, token optimization
  • Core insight: AI agents need more than raw data access; they require an organizational context layer to understand team intent, architecture, and history in order to produce mergeable code.

  - Levels 5-6: MCP + skills, Harness engineering (Context layer).
  - Levels 7-8: Cloud agents, Software factories.
- **Examples**:
  - Moving from GitHub Copilot tab-complete up to automated software factories.
- **Terminology**:
  - AI maturity curve
  - MCP
  - context layer
  - software factories
- **Why it matters**: Most engineering organizations are currently stuck at levels 4 to 5 and treat context as the primary bottleneck.
### Access Does Not Equal Understanding
- **Explanation**: Connecting agents to Model Context Protocols (MCP) gives them access to code and docs, but suffers from 'satisfaction of search' similar to radiologists stopping at one X-ray indicator.
- **Key claims**:
  - Access to information does not equal understanding.
  - Dumping an entire codebase and all docs into a context window causes agent distraction and wastes tokens.
  - Task-specific flow is required to prevent agents from getting distracted.
- **Examples**:
  - Radiologist finding one cancer indicator and missing others; agents finding one piece of info and stopping prematurely.
- **Terminology**:
  - satisfaction of search
  - context window
  - task-specific flow
- **Why it matters**: Unstructured massive context dumps lead to wasted tokens, distracted agents, and operating on wrong assumptions.
### Live Demo: Unblocked with Claude Code and Slack
- **Explanation**: Demonstrating how querying Unblocked directly in Slack or inside Claude Code yields architecturally sound plans, dependency tracing, and accurate context retrieval.
- **Key claims**:
  - Unblocked generates internal diagrams and architectural proposals by understanding code changes and past discussions.
  - Using Unblocked with Claude Code results in ~50% fewer tokens, faster triage, and better answers.
  - Seniority and expertise signals are used to boost important comments in code reviews.
- **Examples**:
  - Asking how the SourceMark engine works and getting a generated pipeline diagram and step-by-step sequencing plan.
  - Debugging why code review issues dropped using Slack conversation threads correlated with PRs.
- **Terminology**:
  - SourceMark engine
  - Context Engine Simulator
  - code review agent
  - engineering social graph
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates measurable cost and time reductions when pairing coding agents with an active context layer.
## Key Points
### Agents as New Employees
- **Explanation**: AI coding agents reset their knowledge on every new task, requiring rediscovery of codebases, test suites, and deployment patterns.
- **Evidence**: Analogy comparing agents to expert software engineers who onboard for the first time on every task.
- **Practical implication**: Engineering teams must provide persistent context layers to prevent repetitive onboarding overhead.
### Access vs Understanding
- **Explanation**: Giving agents raw access to repos via MCPs allows them to search, but they lack holistic understanding of architectural dependencies.
- **Evidence**: Radiology analogy of 'satisfaction of search' where finding one indicator causes an agent to stop searching.
- **Practical implication**: Context engines must curate and route precise information rather than dumping raw codebases into context windows.
### Compounding Cost of Contextless Agents
- **Explanation**: Without upfront context preparation, agents iterate on wrong assumptions, leading to compounding token costs and repeated human intervention.
- **Evidence**: Cost comparison showing session usage with Unblocked (~$0.93, 1 min) versus without Unblocked (~$1.22, 2 mins).
- **Practical implication**: Context layers save significant token costs and wall-clock time on complex multi-step coding tasks.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Levels of AI Maturity in Engineering Organizations
- **How it works**: Categorizes adoption from simple auto-complete to autonomous software factories based on how context is provided to developers and agents.
- **Components**:
  - Tab complete
  - Agent IDE
  - Context engineering
  - Parallel agents
  - MCP + skills
  - Harness engineering
  - Cloud agents
  - Software factories
- **When to use**: To evaluate an engineering team's current readiness and identify bottlenecks in AI adoption.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Asking Claude Code to optimize the SourceMark calculator scheduler with and without Unblocked context.
- **Illustrates**: The difference in plan quality, precision of file references, and token efficiency when using an organizational context engine.
- **Lesson**: Context engines provide precise sequencing plans that avoid unnecessary file scanning and reduce token consumption.
### Analyzing a drop in weekly code review issues by correlating GitHub pull requests with Slack conversations.
- **Illustrates**: How unblocked code review agents leverage historical team conversations and seniority signals.
- **Lesson**: Organizational intelligence extends beyond source code into team communication history.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Evaluate your team's position on the AI maturity curve.
  - Recognize that raw MCP access to code and docs is insufficient for autonomous agents.
  - Test the Context Engine Simulator to measure token and quality differences.
- **Strategic**:
  - Build or adopt a dedicated context layer to prevent agents from resetting knowledge per task.
  - Incorporate organizational metadata (Slack, PRs, Notion docs) into agent execution workflows.
  - Leverage engineering social graphs to weight code review expertise and intent.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can we minimize token costs while scaling agent context windows?
  - What data sources provide the highest signal-to-noise ratio for our engineering agents?
  - How do we maintain security and privacy when feeding organizational chat history into context layers?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Using Unblocked with Claude Code results in ~50% fewer tokens and faster triage. (Performance metric)
- Context engines reduce session costs from $1.22 to $0.93 on complex refactoring tasks. (Cost comparison)
## Notable Quotes
> "AI-generated code should feel like it was written by someone who's been on your team for years. But it doesn't today."
> "For years, you have been the context layer."
> "Now your agents have the same problem. Only the cost compounds."
> "Access to information does not equal understanding."
> "-50% fewer tokens, faster triage, and Unblocked's answer was actually better because it wasn't buried in noise."
## Compressed Summary
- AI agents suffer from onboarding amnesia on every new task.
- Raw MCP access to code and docs leads to distraction and 'satisfaction of search'.
- Unblocked's context engine integrates Slack, GitHub, Notion, and Confluence into agent workflows.
- Context engines reduce token usage by ~50% and wall-clock execution time.
- Engineering social graphs capture tribal knowledge and team seniority signals.
- **Keywords**: context engine, ai agents, mcp, code review, token optimization
- **Core insight**: AI agents need more than raw data access; they require an organizational context layer to understand team intent, architecture, and history in order to produce mergeable code.
